newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam state telecoms unit set to float shares.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam state telecoms unit set to float shares.

text.p: A subsidiary of the state-owned Vietnam Post and Telecommunications Corporation (VNPT) said on Tuesday that it plans to sell 49 percent of its equity to private individuals.

Nguyen Thanh Canh, director of the telecoms equipment and cable manufacturer SACOM, told Reuters that 240,000 shares would be sold at 500,000 dong ($42.90) each in early June if the "equitisation" plan wins government approval.
"This is the right way forward for our development," Canh said. "Once we do the equitisation, we can be sure of our capital and our output."
He said that the state would retain a 51 percent share in SACOM, whose turnover was 71 billion dong in 1996.
Fifteen percent of the shares would be sold to company employees and 34 percent would be allocated to other workers, probably employees in the post and telecoms industry.
Vietnam's ruling Communist Party has called in recent months for a drive to quicken the pace of partial privatisation, or equitisation, in the country's ailing state sector.
The number of state-owned firms has been halved to some 6,250 during the past decade of reform along market lines, but since 1992, just 10 have sold part of their equity to private interests.
Official press reports in the past week have stressed the success of those 10 companies and said that 110 others had registered to follow suit.

Despite the momentum for reform, many in the party and many of the public sector's middle managers still feel uncomfortable with the idea that the state should relinquish control of key economic sectors.

At a policy-defining conference last year, the party affirmed that the state sector's "leading role" would be safeguarded. But it scrapped an original plan to raise the sector's share of economic output to 60 percent from around 40-45 percent now.
Vietnam's aid donors have put strong pressure on Vietnam to reform state-owned companies, many of which are unproductive, unprofitable and saddled with bank debts they cannot repay.
A report in the daily Vietnam News in December said that 70 percent of all public sector companies suffered a loss in 1996.
